Principle · 1 min read

Simplicity

Distilling complex ideas into clear and impactful solutions.

Omarani

The studio's name is the principle. Basata means simplicity.

ba·sa·ta · noun

The philosophy of keeping things simple and clear while focusing on what's most important.

Simple is not the same as empty. It is a discipline:

Supreme simplicity is the discipline of removing everything that is not essential.

01 Four rules of simplicity

I wrote these for untangling a large brand. They hold for a single logo too.

01

One meaning

Stand for one thing deeply, or many things weakly. Not both.

02

Fewer parts, stronger system

Every additional part is a tax on understanding.

03

Consistency over creativity

The recognized brand is the most consistent one, not the most clever.

04

What you remove defines you

A brand is shaped by its disciplined refusals, not its additions.

02 Where the work really is

Most organizations only see the top layer. The work is in the bottom two.
ExpressionWhat people see: the logo, the campaign
SystemThe rules that keep it consistent
FoundationWhat the brand stands for

A simple surface is the result of a clear foundation and a small system. Polish on top can't fix what is missing underneath.

03 In the work: TheChain

TheChain's brief listed eight brand values, seventeen keywords and six possible symbols. That is 31 things to say.

→

One line in the client's own answers held the idea worth keeping: "a chain is only as strong as its weakest link." The mark says that one thing. Six diamonds in a ring, the centre left empty: links with no lock.

04 Try it on your next brief

  1. Say it in one sentence. What does this brand actually stand for, in one sentence that every employee, customer and competitor would agree on?
  2. Count the parts. Every one you add is a tax on understanding.
  3. Remove, then look again. What you remove defines you.

One clear title. One supporting line. Then stop.

Principle · 2 min read

Creativity

Visually and strategically compelling work.

Omarani

Creativity is our cornerstone, driving us to deliver visually and strategically compelling work.

Both words matter. A beautiful identity that solves nothing fails. So does a correct one nobody remembers.

Visually compelling

Beautiful.

It earns attention and holds it.

Strategically compelling

Effective.

It does the job the brand needs done.

We pride ourselves on crafting visual identities that are not only beautiful but also strategic and effective.

01 Excellence is a process

Process is necessary. Process is class. Knowing what to look for, and doing more of it, raises the level at which you can solve problems.

01Curious empathy
02Define
03Ideate
04Play with it
05Test

↻ Tests redefine the problem. Then you loop.

Supported by diligent research and fearless iteration, we explore many possibilities before arriving at a comprehensive and versatile identity system.

Sometimes, the idea reveals itself early but you must research against it.

02 Taste is built

Taste isn't a gift you're born with. It builds up through repetition, one step at a time.

CopySteal
Take one source and reproduce its surface.Take ten sources, understand why each one works, and combine them.
The result belongs to someone else.The result is your signature.

Copy or steal: the idea is Austin Kleon's, from Steal Like an Artist.

03 Two friends before any client

I send every logo to a couple of friends before it goes to the client. They give me just the right feedback, or show me a truly useful blind spot. Excellence needs a second pair of eyes before the client's.

04 In the work: Xaraash

One stroke, two lobes: a hand-drawn X built on a square. Around it sits a system in seven parts.

MarkColourTypeLanguageThe printed worldCampaignProduct

Twelve category icons are drawn to the same stroke. The beauty and the system are the same decision.

05 Patience

If you have 6 hours to cut a tree, spend the first 5 sharpening your saw.

A proverb I keep close.

Sweet results require patience and a taste.

Principle · 2 min read

Impact

Measured by the tangible results our solutions provide.

Omarani

We focus on creating work that truly makes a difference for our clients. Our success is measured by the tangible results and benefits our solutions provide.

Impact is the best thing one can focus on.

Results are not coincidences. They come from solving the right problem.

01 Diagnose before you design

Great craft still fails if it solves the wrong problem.
Make me a flyer→OK!→Flyer, revisions ×5→Problem still there
Make me a flyer→Ask why→The real problem→The right answer, maybe not a flyer

Feedback is a brief in disguise. "Make the logo bigger." Why? "People can't find our shop." That's the real problem.

02 Measure before you strategize

We cannot strategize what we have not measured.

We cannot align without shared evidence.

We cannot lead what we do not yet understand.

The audit is not the strategy. The audit is what makes a real strategy possible.

03 Start with the audience

When you are building a brand, you're building an entity to connect a business with an audience. No shiny brand identity or logo will get the job done. You need to first understand what that audience wants.

The four-people test

→One message

Before you call a piece finished, ask: would four different people get the same message from it?

04 Find the difference

The market is noise. Nobody can hear "better". What gets noticed is different.

The onlyness test

Our [offering] is the only [category] that [benefit].

If you can't fill in the blanks, you haven't found the difference yet.

The zag and the onlyness test are Marty Neumeier's.

A brand that knows where it's going is more likely to get there.

05 In the work: the National Transformation Plan

Fifteen transformation labs in three families had to carry one identity: six economic, five social, four enabling.

6Economic
5Social
4Enabling
1Mark

Each blade of the star is drawn from fine lines: fifteen labs, one direction.

The result

On launch day the mark was carried on the scarf, the stage and the outdoor campaign.

Principle · 1 min read

Integrity

Trust through transparency, reliability and respect.

Omarani

Honesty and ethical conduct are paramount in all our dealings. We build trust through transparency, reliability, and respect for everyone we work with.

reliable+on time+honest=reputation

Clients forget the colours. They remember whether you were reliable, whether you delivered on time, and whether you were honest with them.

01 Care before the sale

I love interviewing founders, getting to know them, with a white note page and a present brain, full of curiosity.

Asking deep questions about their project, their thought process, their market understanding. Walking them through my process, clarifying everything they ask with honesty and no expectation of a sale. Showing someone actual care about what they are about to pay you for convinces them you're worth paying.

Communication must be co-created, not imposed.

02 Slow-cooked

I hate anything that's urgent and can't be slow-cooked. It wasn't worth it.

Rushed

You end up assuming instead of asking.

Slow-cooked

Room to think. Room to ask why.

Anything that can't be slow-cooked isn't mine to cook.

03 Defend every decision

"Blue, because I like it."

A preference. The client can have a different one, and then it's their taste against yours.

"Blue, because…"

A reason, standing on three legs: the audience, the visual hierarchy, and the brief.

The decision
AudienceVisual hierarchyThe brief

04 Consistency is integrity

Consistency drives the power and integrity of a brand.

A brand that keeps its word in every place it appears earns trust the same way a person does.

The brand is not what we say. It is what survives when we stop talking.

05 The value, not the name

My goal is never to glorify myself. The point is the value.

Love your craft and it will love you back.

Article · 6 min read

Understood: one word for how designers think

Craft, diagnose, present. Three jobs, one test: was it understood?

Omarani

You know the tools. Is that enough?

Of course not.

That is how I opened a guest lecture at Alamtara. Laptops closed. Phones away. A room of creatives who had finished the course and knew the software.

You can't read about push-ups and get strong, and knowing the software doesn't make you a designer.

The lesson is about the other part. How designers think. I prepared it for junior creatives. Here it is written down, for designers who already know the tools.

It has three parts. When I cut it down to fit one hour, I found all three come down to one word.

Understood.

  1. Craft: make work that is understood.
  2. Diagnose: understand the client before you design.
  3. Present: get your idea understood.
PartThe jobThe check
01 CraftMake work that is understoodWould four different people get the same message from it?
02 DiagnoseUnderstand the client before you designDid you ask why, or assume?
03 PresentGet your idea understoodDoes every decision stand on a reason, not a preference?

01 Craft: make work that is understood

Draw a fence

Is design an art? Start by drawing a fence between the two.

ArtDesign
Talent, taste and self-expression.Visual communication and problem-solving with type, space, image and colour.
Art is interpreted.Design is understood.
It sends a different message to everyone who sees it. That's its value.It sends the same message to everyone.
Neither is better. They do different jobs, and a client is paying for the second one.

The four-people test

Before you call a piece finished, ask: would four different people get the same message from it?

Words are not writing

Line, shape, form, texture, colour, type. You already know the elements. They're your vocabulary.

Elements are the words. Principles are the grammar.

But knowing words doesn't make you a writer. What turns vocabulary into answers is a process.

A process you can run

  1. Curious empathy. Learn who you're speaking to before you draw anything. You can't hit a target you can't see.
  2. Define. Write down the real problem in one sentence.
  3. Ideate. Generate options against that problem, not against your taste.
  4. Play with it. Prototype on one real surface.
  5. Test. Put it in front of people.
It isn't a straight line, it's a loop.

Testing shows you something the brief never mentioned. That redefines the problem. So you go round again.

The same loop, for identity work

In my Alamtara branding session I ran the loop on identity. The labels change. The logic doesn't.

StepFor identity
Curious empathyLearn who you're speaking for before you draw a mark.
DefineWrite the judgment line, the rule you'll keep when asked for "more."
IdeateGenerate options against the judgment, not against taste.
Play with itPrototype the system on one real surface they actually ship.
TestStress-test: can a teammate apply it without you in the room?

Audience → Judgment → Options → One surface → Lock.

Consistency of judgment beats a clever mark.

The first step is the one I love most. From my own notes:

I love interviewing founders, getting to know them, with a white note page and a present brain, full of curiosity.

And the test step is not only for the end:

Sometimes, the idea reveals itself early but you must research against it

Taste is built, day by day

The loop tells you what to do. Taste tells you when it's good.

Taste isn't a gift you're born with. It builds up through repetition, one step at a time.

"Sweet results require patience and a taste."

"Care arrives before the invoice does."

Then there is the question of where taste comes from. Copy or steal. The idea is Austin Kleon's, from Steal Like an Artist.

CopySteal
Take one source and reproduce its surface.Take ten sources, understand why each one works, and combine them.
The result belongs to someone else.The result is your signature.

Think about it

You hit a creative wall on a tight deadline. What's the first thing you do?

In the room, I asked this and held seven seconds of silence. Hold it for yourself too.

02 Diagnose: understand before you design

Great craft still fails if it solves the wrong problem. So who decides what the problem is?

When everyone zigs, zag

The market is noise. Too many products, features, ads, messages and channels, all pushing in the same direction. Nobody can hear "better". What gets noticed is different.

It's better to be different than better.

That line I credit to Chris Do. The zag is Marty Neumeier's. So is the test that goes with it.

The onlyness test

Can you finish this sentence?

Our [offering] is the only [category] that [benefit].

If you can't fill in the blanks, you haven't found the difference yet, whether for a client or for yourself as a designer.

Nobody asks a question

A client says, "Make me a flyer." The junior designer says "OK!", makes the flyer, and does five rounds of revisions. Everyone stays comfortable and nobody asks a question. The flyer ships, and the real business problem is still there.

Make me a flyer→OK!→Flyer, revisions ×5→Problem still there
Make me a flyer→Ask why→The real problem→The right answer, maybe not a flyer

Don't ask "What do you want me to make?" Ask why first. Never assume you know the answer before the client finishes talking.

The answers lead to the real problem, and from there to the right answer.

Sometimes that answer isn't a flyer at all.

#AskDontAssume

Reputation is slow-cooked

Clients forget the colours. They remember whether you were reliable, whether you delivered on time, and whether you were honest with them.

reliable + on time + honest = reputation

Good work also needs room to think. Rushing is how you end up assuming instead of asking.

Anything that can't be slow-cooked isn't mine to cook.

03 Present: get your idea understood

The client wasn't in your head.

Now the idea has to survive the meeting.

A great idea nobody remembers is a failed idea.

Five things that make an idea stick

This is Patrick Winston's star.

  1. Symbol: one image people can hold on to.
  2. Slogan: a short handle they can repeat.
  3. Surprise: something that breaks an assumption.
  4. Salient idea: the one thing that stands out.
  5. Story: the problem, what you discovered, and the solution.
The reveal: the lecture was a star

I built the talk on the star, then showed the room at minute 40.

Star pointIn this lesson
SymbolThe fence: art and design
Slogan#AskDontAssume
Surprise"Maybe not a flyer"
Salient ideaDesign is understood
StoryYour story

Defend every decision

"Blue, because I like it."

A preference. The client can have a different one, and then it's their taste against yours.

"Blue, because…"

A reason, standing on three legs: the audience, the visual hierarchy, and the brief.

Feedback is a brief in disguise.

AI and you

AI is good at research, building personas, and producing lots of ideas fast. It can't supply taste, curious empathy or judgment. Those still have to come from you.

AI is not going to replace you. Designers using AI are going to reach heights nobody else reached.

AI can make the slides. Only you can give the reasons.

What to take with you

  1. Design is understood. Solve the problem and send one clear message.
  2. Diagnose before you design. Ask why. Don't assume.
  3. Get your idea understood. Package it well, defend it with reasons, and use AI with taste.

On Monday

On your next brief, before you open any software, ask why and write the real problem in one sentence.

Thinking like a designer = making things understood.

Article · 4 min read

Identity is a set of craft refusals

Brand is not the logo. It's the judgment you keep when someone asks for “more.”

Omarani

I ran a guest session at Alamtara on branding and identity. The title slide said it in three words.

Process, not polish!

The session was a walk through one process. The judgment process that turns a promise into a recognizable brand identity. Not a moodboard.

It opens with a question.

So finishing the logo is enough?

Of course not.

01 The frame: brand is not the logo

Here is the definition I gave the room.

Branding is judgment made recognizable, a small system of rules that keep a promise consistent across every surface.

Read it slowly. There are four parts in that sentence.

PartWhat it means
JudgmentThe decisions come first. The mark comes after.
A small system of rulesFew pieces. Hard rules.
A promiseThe thing the rules protect.
Every surfaceConsistent everywhere it shows up, not only on the logo sheet.

The logo is one output of that system. It isn't the system.

02 The line you keep

Every identity gets the same request sooner or later. More.

More colour. More elements. One more line on the cover. That is where the identity is decided. Not at the logo presentation.

So in my process the Define step has one job.

Write the judgment line, the rule you'll keep when asked for "more."

That's the refusal written down before anyone asks. Everything else in the process leans on it.

03 A process you can run, for identity

It's the same design thinking loop I teach for any design work. Five steps. My labels.

  1. Curious empathy. Learn who you're speaking for before you draw a mark.
  2. Define. Write the judgment line, the rule you'll keep when asked for "more."
  3. Ideate. Generate options against the judgment, not against taste.
  4. Play with it. Prototype the system on one real surface they actually ship.
  5. Test. Stress-test: can a teammate apply it without you in the room?
It isn't a straight line, it's a loop.

Tests reveal insights that redefine the problem. Then you loop.

General loopFor identity
EmpathizeAudience
DefineJudgment
IdeateOptions
PrototypeOne surface
TestLock

Speaking for, not speaking to

In the general lesson, curious empathy means learning who you're speaking to. You can't hit a target you can't see.

For identity I changed one word. Learn who you're speaking for. The brand speaks on someone's behalf. You need to know them before you draw a mark.

Options against the judgment

The Ideate step is where most identity work drifts. Options get made against taste. Mine, the client's, whoever is loudest in the room.

The judgment line gives the options something to be measured against.

The loop tells you what to do. Taste tells you when it's good.

Taste still has a job. It just isn't the brief.

One real surface

Play with it means one surface they actually ship. Not a mockup wall. The system has to survive contact with a real thing.

The test without you

Can a teammate apply it without you in the room?

If the answer is no, the rules live in your head, not in the system.

It's the identity version of a check from the lesson:

Before you call a piece finished, ask: would four different people get the same message from it?

Four people reading it. One teammate applying it. Same idea. One message, kept.

04 Three refusals

The deck has three do-and-don't slides. Read them as refusals.

I refuseInstead
Logo dump, marks with no rulesSystem, few pieces, hard rules. Name, voice, type, colour.
Moodboard as strategyShip one surface under the system. One surface. One judgment. Locked.
Crowded, everything shoutsQuiet hierarchy, one idea wins. One clear title. One supporting line. Then stop.
What "crowded" looked like on the slide

TITLE TITLE TITLE!!!

subtitle and also a tagline and also another line

CTA · CTA · CTA · MORE

body body body body body body body

#tag #tag #tag #tag #tag

logo · logo · badge · seal

That's what "more" looks like when nobody holds the line.

05 Craft refusals

This is the line the whole session was built to land.

Identity is a set of craft refusals, what you will not change once you know who you're speaking for.

Notice the order. First you know who you're speaking for. Then you decide what you won't change. The refusal comes out of the empathy. It isn't stubbornness.

Consistency of judgment beats a clever mark.

Defend the refusal with reasons

A refusal only holds if you can say why. In the lesson I put it like this.

"Blue, because I like it."

A preference. The client can have a different one, and then it's their taste against yours.

"Blue, because…"

A reason, standing on three legs: the audience, the visual hierarchy, and the brief.

When someone asks for "more", the judgment line is the reason. Not your taste.

06 Start this week

Start with judgment. Keep the system small. Ship one surface this week.

The session ended on a worksheet. Three lines. Fill them in before you open any software.

  1. Audience. Who is this for, one concrete sentence?
  2. Judgment line. The rule you'll keep when asked for "more."
  3. Surface. One real surface you'll ship under the system today.

Omarani

A client says, "Make me a flyer." The designer says "OK!", makes the flyer, does five rounds of revisions. Nobody asks a question, and the problem is still there.

Note · 1 min read

Speed is not the craft

On process, AI and patience.

Omarani

I don't respect designers who brag about how fast they come up with ideas.

I love those who give creativity its due. Those who look for inspiration, walk to get ideas, sketch like there's no tomorrow, sleep on ideas and look again with fresh eyes. Those who never assume they know the answer before the client finishes talking.

AI can help you come up with cooler stuff you couldn't do alone. That doesn't say do it quick.

Process is necessary. Process is class. Knowing what to look for, and doing more of it, raises the level at which you can solve problems.

Sweet results require patience and a taste.

Note · 1 min read

Notes on a signature

Process notes for designers who already know the craft.

Omarani

These are notes, not a method.

My goal is never to glorify myself. The point is the value.

The work is mine

I treat my work as mine, not a mere project. That didn't happen in one moment. It built up over time.

Two friends before any client

I have a couple of friends I send every logo to before it goes to the client. They give me just the right feedback, or show me a truly useful blind spot. Some interpret the design better than I intended it. That helps when I prepare my presentations.

A logo I loved

As a junior designer, I made one of three options presented to a client. I was really in love with that logo. Eight years later, I still believe it was the most suitable solution for their brief. They took a colleague's design, so I put mine as my desktop wallpaper to give it the love it deserved. I kept it about two months, until I became familiar with it, and let it go.
